short: The largest British offensive of 1915, notable for their first use of poison gas and devastating infantry losses.
full:
Intended to support a massive French offensive in Champagne, the British Army launched an attack near the coal-mining town of Loos on 25 September 1915. Hoping to overcome strong German defensive positions, the British released chlorine gas prior to the assault. However, shifting winds blew the gas back into their own trenches, causing confusion and casualties among the advancing troops.

Despite initial breakthroughs that captured the town of Loos, the offensive quickly faltered due to a lack of reserves and inadequate artillery support. When fresh British divisions were finally sent forward on the second day, they advanced in dense formations against uncut barbed wire and intact machine-gun nests, suffering horrific losses. The failure at Loos led to the replacement of Sir John French by Sir Douglas Haig as commander of the British Expeditionary Force.
